avibase-09A0F2EB.name: African Crake
avibase-09A0F2EB.text: This crake lives in grasslands across much of sub-Saharan Africa. Seasonal rains draw it to places where the grass has grown tall enough for nesting.

avibase-66931B3F.name: African Cuckoo
avibase-66931B3F.text: Its migrations stay within Africa, often following the rains. Listen for the male’s paired, deep “coo” notes, with the second sometimes more emphatic.

sources.title: Peacock (2014): Identifying Common and African Cuckoos
Atlas of Southern African Birds: African Cuckoo

avibase-40A2405D.name: African Thrush
avibase-40A2405D.text: A resident of wooded Africa, from Senegal eastwards and south into Angola and Zambia. Its orange-yellow bill stands out against a grey-brown head and back.

sources.title: Adang 2018: Breeding biology of the African Thrush

avibase-CDA2E56B.name: American Pipit
avibase-CDA2E56B.text: A North American pipit with a buff breast and fine streaks. It spends much of its time on the ground, where its grey-brown back can be easy to overlook.

avibase-32E65FB3.name: Ashy Bulbul
avibase-32E65FB3.text: Grey feathers cover the back and breast, giving this bulbul its ashy appearance. A white throat and a bright yellow patch on the wing interrupt the grey.

avibase-8D1CF2FF.name: Ashy Woodpecker
avibase-8D1CF2FF.text: The back and wings are grey-brown to dark slate, with a pale buff underside. Males add a red face; females have a grey head instead.

sources.title: Oiseaux-Birds: Ashy Woodpecker, text by Nicole Bouglouan and photographs by Roger Ahlman

avibase-E0ED3A27.name: Banded Barbet
avibase-E0ED3A27.text: Look for the bands across its underside and rump. This stocky barbet lives in Ethiopia and Eritrea, using its heavy bill to eat fruit and excavate nest holes.

avibase-303D5356.name: Banded Kingfisher
avibase-303D5356.text: Both sexes have bands, but in different colours. The male’s back is striped black and blue; the female’s head and back are patterned black and reddish brown.

sources.title: MyBIS: Birds of Malaysia (2016), page 50, photographs by Muhammad Al Zahri

avibase-05CFB3D1.name: Banded Woodpecker
avibase-05CFB3D1.text: Dark bars cross its pale belly, with more barring on the reddish breast. Above, the bird is mostly rusty brown, topped by a shaggy yellowish nape.

avibase-6BBBDB1A.name: Banded Wren
avibase-6BBBDB1A.text: Black bars mark the wings, tail, lower belly and sides. The back is chestnut brown, while a bold white stripe runs above each eye.

sources.title: Alexander Skutch 1940: Social and sleeping habits of Central American wrens

avibase-C39D115A.name: Barred Hawk
avibase-C39D115A.text: Fine dark bars cross the pale belly and underwings, below a dark chest. Seen from above, this hawk looks mostly dark, with a white band on the tail.

avibase-148F0B01.name: Black Crake
avibase-148F0B01.text: The adult is mostly black, with a yellow bill, red eyes and red legs. Young birds are browner, so the name fits the adult more closely.

sources.title: Newman’s Birds of Southern Africa: Black Crake

avibase-EDB84334.name: Black Cuckoo
avibase-EDB84334.text: Mostly black, sometimes with faint barring underneath. The male’s repeated three-note call rises at the end and is often remembered as “I’m so sick”.

sources.title: Newman’s Birds of Southern Africa: Black Cuckoo

avibase-A41CD4E7.name: Black Harrier
avibase-A41CD4E7.text: A perched adult can look almost entirely black. Flight reveals a white rump and pale flight feathers; young birds have buff underparts and a streaked chest.

avibase-74853F89.name: Black Heron
avibase-74853F89.text: Black feathers, a black bill and yellow feet make this heron distinctive. When fishing, it spreads its wings into a dark canopy over the water.

avibase-811FC719.name: Black Lark
avibase-811FC719.text: The breeding male is almost all black, with a pale bill. The female looks quite different: she is mottled grey above and much paler below.

avibase-ADD8E888.name: Black Monarch
avibase-ADD8E888.text: “Monarch” is the bird family here. This forest bird lives in New Guinea’s highlands and is also called the Black Monarch Flycatcher.

sources.title: Incubation behaviour and parental care of a nestling in the Black Monarch

avibase-0C95D04B.name: Black Thrush
avibase-0C95D04B.text: Adult males are black, with a bright yellow bill and eye-ring. Females are olive-brown, and young birds are brown with spots on their underparts.

sources.title: Smithsonian Institution: specimen description of Planesticus infuscatus

avibase-1C98EA2F.name: Black Wheatear
avibase-1C98EA2F.text: The male is black except for a white rump and largely white tail. The female has the same pattern, but her dark feathers are brown.

sources.title: Madrid: Catalogue of species at Casa de Campo (2015)

avibase-C72EC8C8.name: Black-headed Bulbul
avibase-C72EC8C8.text: A glossy blue-black head sits above an olive-yellow body. Some birds have grey bodies instead, but the dark head and lack of a crest remain useful clues.

sources.title: Bird Society of Singapore: Black-headed Bulbul

avibase-19D053B3.name: Black-headed Weaver
avibase-19D053B3.text: The black head belongs to the breeding male, framed by a yellow collar. Females and males outside the breeding season lack that dark head pattern.

avibase-12CA8603.name: Black-headed Woodpecker
avibase-12CA8603.text: Black on the face contrasts with a yellow throat and green wings. The male has a red crown; the female’s crown is entirely black.

sources.title: Craig Robson: Field Guide to the Birds of Thailand, publisher preview

avibase-DEEC38A7.name: Blue-winged Parrot
avibase-DEEC38A7.text: Deep blue covers much of the male’s wing, against an olive-green body and yellow belly. Females are duller and have a smaller area of blue.

avibase-AA127B89.name: Blue-winged Pitta
avibase-AA127B89.text: Bright blue wings sit between a green back and reddish undertail. This short-tailed pitta also has a black head, a pale eyebrow and a white throat.

sources.title: Bird Society of Singapore: Blue-winged Pitta

avibase-457C01A2.name: Brown Crake
avibase-457C01A2.text: Olive-brown upperparts and brown flanks surround a greyer face and breast. It lives in vegetated wetlands, including reedbeds and irrigation channels. Males and females look alike.

sources.title: Journal on New Biological Reports: Brown Crake observations

avibase-4D5D2BC3.name: Brown Skua
avibase-4D5D2BC3.text: In New Zealand it is often called the Subantarctic Skua, a dark-brown bird with broad wings and white flashes that show in flight.

sources.title: New Zealand Birds Online: Subantarctic Skua
Department of Conservation: Birds of the Chatham Islands

avibase-93CA037F.name: Caspian Gull
avibase-93CA037F.text: It breeds around the Black and Caspian Seas and east across Central Asia. Its long, slender bill and sloping forehead give it a distinctive profile.

sources.title: British Trust for Ornithology: Caspian Gull

avibase-264D0351.name: Caspian Plover
avibase-264D0351.text: Its breeding grounds include open country north and east of the Caspian Sea. After breeding, this long-legged plover travels south to eastern and southern Africa.

avibase-BC06BC0D.name: Caspian Tern
avibase-BC06BC0D.text: Named for the Caspian Sea, yet found around much of the world. It is the largest tern, with a heavy orange-red bill and a black cap.

sources.title: HANZAB: Caspian Tern, via New Zealand Birds Online

avibase-5BAE0043.name: Chestnut Bulbul
avibase-5BAE0043.text: Also called the Chestnut-backed Bulbul. This bird lives mainly in the humid forest canopy in southern China and northern Vietnam.

sources.title: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society: Chestnut Bulbul

avibase-01BFAE61.name: Chestnut Weaver
avibase-01BFAE61.text: The breeding male has a rich chestnut body and a black head. Females and non-breeding males are browner, with a buff or chestnut band across the breast.

avibase-9DD65284.name: Chestnut Woodpecker
avibase-9DD65284.text: Deep chestnut colours cover much of its head and body. Males have a bright red cheek stripe; females lack the red, while crest colour varies between populations.

avibase-D3B8C7BE.name: Collared Babbler
avibase-D3B8C7BE.text: Its collar can be faint or absent. Where clear, it appears as a dark patch on each side of the breast, against buff underparts.

sources.title: N. J. Collar: revision of Asian babblers

avibase-0B2F8058.name: Collared Flycatcher
avibase-0B2F8058.text: The breeding male wears a white collar between his black head and back. Outside the breeding season, his plumage becomes browner, and females are brown too.

sources.title: British Birds: Photographic studies of Collared Flycatcher

avibase-F7B5C386.name: Collared Grosbeak
avibase-F7B5C386.text: The male has an orange-tinged yellow collar between his black head and bright yellow body. Females are olive-green above and yellowish below, without his black face.

sources.title: Knowler (1993): Collared Grosbeak Mycerobas affinis, a new species for Thailand, Forktail 8:152–153

avibase-5DA28D37.name: Collared Kingfisher
avibase-5DA28D37.text: A white collar separates the head from the blue-green back. Females tend to look greener than males, and young birds have darker, scaly markings on the neck.

avibase-EABE979B.name: Collared Myna
avibase-EABE979B.text: A broad white collar crosses the sides and back of this myna’s neck. The head is black, with a small crest above the bill.

sources.title: Banmaw University Research Journal: bird survey

avibase-D0AA9105.name: Collared Nightjar
avibase-D0AA9105.text: Its scientific genus, Gactornis, starts with G, A, C and T: the letters used for DNA’s four bases. “Ornis” adds the Greek word for bird.

sources.title: Han, Robbins and Braun (2010): A multi-gene estimate of phylogeny in the nightjars and nighthawks
Martens and Bahr: new bird taxa for 2010

avibase-03D0649C.name: Collared Plover
avibase-03D0649C.text: The adult’s collar is a narrow black band across the breast. In young birds the band is often incomplete, so the full pattern develops with age.

avibase-1611F295.name: Collared Sunbird
avibase-1611F295.text: The male’s yellow belly is topped by a narrow purple breast band. His head and back are glossy green; the female lacks the band.

sources.title: Kloof Conservancy: Collared Sunbird, Highway Mail (2022)

avibase-310AEDC8.name: Common Babbler
avibase-310AEDC8.text: Its long tail is a useful clue: the Common Babbler is a slim, streaky bird of dry scrub, found mainly in India.

sources.title: Bird Count India: The Jungle Babbler and its Six Sisters

avibase-00DA9D91.name: Common Gull
avibase-00DA9D91.text: Despite its name, the Common Gull is uncommon in much of inland Britain. It can gather in large numbers on the coast.

avibase-9505E03D.name: Common Kingfisher
avibase-9505E03D.text: Also called the Eurasian or River Kingfisher. It has a blue-green back and rusty-orange underside, and occurs across much of Eurasia and North Africa.

sources.title: Singapore National Parks: What Is That Blue Bird

avibase-407E2CA8.name: Common Merganser
avibase-407E2CA8.text: Common Merganser and Goosander are two names for the same fish-eating duck. The first is usual in North America, the second in Eurasia.

avibase-4E6EF3F9.name: Common Swift
avibase-4E6EF3F9.text: Its scientific name, Apus apus, comes from an ancient word meaning “without feet”. Swifts do have feet, but their very short legs are mostly used for clinging.

avibase-4D2FF6F1.name: Common Tern
avibase-4D2FF6F1.text: Its long tail has earned it the nickname “sea-swallow”. Silvery-grey above and white below, it hovers over water before diving for fish.

sources.title: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds: Common Tern

avibase-546FA5F2.name: Crested Barbet
avibase-546FA5F2.text: A small black crest rises from a head speckled red and yellow. Its bright belly, spotted wings and broad black neck band add to the patchwork.

sources.title: Newman’s Birds of Southern Africa: Crested Barbet

avibase-079F846A.name: Crested Duck
avibase-079F846A.text: Both sexes have a small crest at the back of the head. It is often held so low that it can be hard to see.

sources.title: John Avise, University of California Irvine: Crested Duck

avibase-3E328C3C.name: Crested Ibis
avibase-3E328C3C.text: Long feathers form a dense crest at the back of the head. The bare face is red, while the plumage can show white, pink and seasonal grey.

sources.title: University of Michigan Animal Diversity Web: Nipponia nippon

avibase-BE8DC16C.name: Crested Kingfisher
avibase-BE8DC16C.text: The crest is a large, shaggy spray of black-and-white feathers. This is a big kingfisher, with a heavy bill and fine barring across its back and wings.

avibase-65BCBB64.name: Crested Myna
avibase-65BCBB64.text: Its crest is a tuft on the forehead, just above the bill, rather than a spike at the back. The female’s tuft is slightly less developed.

sources.title: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society: Crested Myna

avibase-245D312A.name: Crested Pigeon
avibase-245D312A.text: A slender black spike stands on top of the head. This Australian pigeon also has metallic wing patches and makes a whistling sound with its wings when startled.

avibase-A977348D.name: Desert Lark
avibase-A977348D.text: This lark favours broken, stony desert ground. Its plumage varies with the landscape, from sandy birds in pale country to much darker birds on basalt.

sources.title: Ornithological Society of the Middle East: Region List, Part C

avibase-F6F87349.name: Desert Owl
avibase-F6F87349.text: The “hadorami” in its scientific name honours Israeli ornithologist Hadoram Shirihai, who noticed differences between this bird and the closely related Omani Owl.

sources.title: Perlman, Blair and Sheldon: Taxonomic advances and mysteries in the OSME Region

avibase-078BC0ED.name: Desert Wheatear
avibase-078BC0ED.text: “Wheatear” comes from an old form of “white arse”, referring to these birds’ pale rumps. This species lives in deserts and semi-deserts across North Africa and Asia.

avibase-775C66B9.name: Dusky Babbler
avibase-775C66B9.text: Its scientific name, tenebrosa, also carries the sense of dark or gloomy. This babbler lives in moist scrub in parts of central and eastern Africa.

avibase-F0258298.name: Dusky Hummingbird
avibase-F0258298.text: Grey underparts give this hummingbird a subdued look. Bronze-green feathers above and a red bill add colour.

sources.title: CONABIO: Aves, account for Cynanthus sordidus

avibase-F1F444EE.name: Dusky Munia
avibase-F1F444EE.text: Dark brown to brown-black all over, with darker feather tips that can look like scales. The upper bill is black and the lower bill blue-grey.

avibase-67D59645.name: Dusky Nightjar
avibase-67D59645.text: Dark brown plumage is scattered with buff, tawny and cinnamon markings. Females can look paler and more reddish than males.

avibase-1A87E3A9.name: Dusky Parrot
avibase-1A87E3A9.text: Dark brown feathers have paler edges. A blue tail and red feathers beneath it add colour to this otherwise dusky parrot.

avibase-A057002F.name: Dusky Pigeon
avibase-A057002F.text: Grey on the head merges into darker brown across the back and wings. The colours are subdued, with little contrast.

avibase-5C54F8C9.name: Dusky Tit
avibase-5C54F8C9.text: The male is black and the female ashy-black, without bright wing patches. Deep red eyes supply a small flash of colour.

sources.title: Nicole Bouglouan: Tits, Chickadees and Titmice

avibase-96819591.name: Dusky Warbler
avibase-96819591.text: Brown plumage makes a quiet backdrop to a bold pale eyebrow. Its sharp face pattern and orange-toned legs help birders pick it out.

sources.title: BirdGuides: Radde’s and Dusky Warblers photo ID guide

avibase-9E8F1FEB.name: Elegant Parrot
avibase-9E8F1FEB.text: A deep blue band crosses the forehead of this yellow-and-olive parrot. Females are generally duller, and young birds have little or none of the blue band.

avibase-1267C963.name: Elegant Pitta
avibase-1267C963.text: This name covers several island forms. Their throat markings range from an extensive black patch to a narrow black line beneath the bill.

sources.title: Yue et al. 2020: Species limits in the Elegant Pitta complex

avibase-E7057C1D.name: Elegant Sunbird
avibase-E7057C1D.text: The male combines a blue-green crown with a purplish-red neck collar and yellow underparts. The female is olive above and yellow below.

avibase-EF7D309C.name: Elegant Tit
avibase-EF7D309C.text: Yellow cheeks and underparts stand out against a black head. Pale spots and wing markings break up its dark back.

avibase-D6F5D224.name: Fairy Flycatcher
avibase-D6F5D224.text: Only about 11 cm long, this little bird has a black eye mask, white eyebrow and a pink wash below. The “flycatcher” part describes its darting trips from a perch to catch insects.

avibase-0ECBA406.name: Fairy Pitta
avibase-0ECBA406.text: Green upperparts, blue wing patches and a warm brown crown make a striking combination. A black eye mask sits between a pale eyebrow and white throat.

sources.title: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society: Fairy Pitta

avibase-C2AD2E83.name: Forest Buzzard
avibase-C2AD2E83.text: Indigenous forests are central to its habitat, although it also uses nearby pine and eucalyptus plantations. It often hunts by dropping from a perch onto prey.

avibase-31B7FC11.name: Forest Kingfisher
avibase-31B7FC11.text: This blue-and-white kingfisher needs forest or woodland for breeding. Much of its hunting happens on land, where it catches insects, small lizards and other prey.

avibase-D2B2A4AF.name: Forest Thrush
avibase-D2B2A4AF.text: A shy bird of Caribbean forests, with a yellow bill, yellow legs and yellow skin around the eye. Its brown-edged belly feathers give it a scaled appearance.

avibase-8E872FAA.name: Forest Wagtail
avibase-8E872FAA.text: Both words fit: it favours shaded woodland paths and moves its tail from side to side. That sideways swing is an unusual wagtail habit.

avibase-F51C1C4A.name: Giant Kingfisher
avibase-F51C1C4A.text: At roughly 44 cm long, it is Africa’s largest kingfisher. Chestnut colour sits on the male’s upper breast, but lower down on the female’s breast and belly.

sources.title: Phil Hockey: Africa’s Kingfishers, University of Cape Town archive

avibase-9569D117.name: Giant Weaver
avibase-9569D117.text: The male carries an exceptionally large bill, the largest among weavers. Its scientific name, grandis, means large or great. This species is native to São Tomé.

avibase-ECCBDBAF.name: Giant Wren
avibase-ECCBDBAF.text: At 20–22 cm long, this is a substantial wren. A white eyebrow and belly contrast with its black crown and rich chestnut back.

sources.title: Cruz-Vázquez and Velázquez-Velázquez: Giant Wren in Oaxaca, Huitzil 21(1)

avibase-3D4BA49D.name: Golden Babbler
avibase-3D4BA49D.text: The golden-yellow crown and nape are traced with fine black streaks. Olive wings and yellow underparts complete the colour scheme.

sources.title: E. C. Stuart Baker: The Fauna of British India, Golden-headed Babbler

avibase-98C0C634.name: Golden Bowerbird
avibase-98C0C634.text: Males take years to acquire their gold. The first yellow feathers appear around the fifth year, with full adult plumage following the next complete moult.

sources.title: Australian Bird Study Association: Golden Bowerbird

avibase-B653A80B.name: Golden Grosbeak
avibase-B653A80B.text: The male is bright yellow, set off by black-and-white wings and tail. Females are duller yellow, with grey upperparts and grey speckles on the head and neck.

avibase-6778547A.name: Golden Monarch
avibase-6778547A.text: The male pairs bright golden yellow with black. Females wear a quieter olive-yellow plumage.

sources.title: Van Balen, Kilmaskossu and Puradyatmika: Birds of Mimika

avibase-589694DD.name: Golden Nightjar
avibase-589694DD.text: Golden-buff feathers set this nightjar apart, though the colour is easier to see in good light. In flight, white wing patches contrast with strongly barred feathers.

sources.title: Dutch Birding: Golden Nightjar in Western Sahara, May 2015

avibase-21BA7041.name: Golden Swallow
avibase-21BA7041.text: Gosse’s 1847 description of the Jamaican bird praised its golden-green gloss. The Hispaniolan bird in this photograph shines blue-green.

sources.title: Philip Henry Gosse: The Birds of Jamaica (1847), Golden Swallow

avibase-49D9148A.name: Great Egret
avibase-49D9148A.text: Much larger than a Little Egret, this bird is roughly the size of a Grey Heron. You may also see it called the Great White Egret.

avibase-EA53492B.name: Great Grebe
avibase-EA53492B.text: South America’s largest grebe dives for food in lakes and coastal waters. In one Argentine lagoon, researchers found it eating more crabs than fish.

sources.title: Josens, Bó and Favero (2010): Foraging ecology of the Great Grebe

avibase-BB041C6E.name: Great Skua
avibase-BB041C6E.text: A large, powerful seabird, dark brown with striking white flashes in its wings. It often chases other seabirds until they give up their catch.

avibase-23C068E4.name: Great Thrush
avibase-23C068E4.text: At 28–33 cm long, this is a large thrush. Orange feet and bill brighten its dark grey-brown plumage; adult males also have a vivid orange eye-ring.

sources.title: Banco de la República / Universidad ICESI: Turdus fuscater

avibase-08DD4E80.name: Green Ibis
avibase-08DD4E80.text: Its dark feathers have a green sheen. The long curved bill and legs are greenish too, so the name is easier to understand in good light.

avibase-ED7D6741.name: Green Kingfisher
avibase-ED7D6741.text: Green above, with a white collar and belly. The male has a chestnut breast band; the female’s band is greenish.

sources.title: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Learn About Texas Birds

avibase-804CCA3A.name: Grey Gull
avibase-804CCA3A.text: Grey covers most of this gull, including its head outside the breeding season. The head turns white when it is breeding, while the body stays grey.

sources.title: Museo de Historia Natural de Concepción: Gaviota Garuma

avibase-943AA4FB.name: Grey Hawk
avibase-943AA4FB.text: Adults are grey, finely barred below, with bold black-and-white tail bands. Young birds look quite different: brown above and streaked underneath.

avibase-7A2734EB.name: Grey Nightjar
avibase-7A2734EB.text: Its grey plumage is broken up by black, silver, white and buff markings. That intricate pattern helps the resting bird blend into its surroundings.

sources.title: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society: Grey Nightjar

avibase-27903EF7.name: Grey Plover
avibase-27903EF7.text: Its winter plumage is brownish-grey. In breeding plumage, silver-and-black markings above contrast with a black face and belly.

avibase-C1CBA33A.name: Grey Sunbird
avibase-C1CBA33A.text: An unusually subdued sunbird. Even the male can resemble a female of more colourful species, although small red tufts at the sides of its chest give him away.

avibase-AE073221.name: Grey Wagtail
avibase-AE073221.text: The grey is on its back. Under the long tail is a bright patch of lemon yellow, a useful mark when the bird is bobbing beside a stream.

avibase-BC75EA9A.name: Grey Waxbill
avibase-BC75EA9A.text: Mostly soft grey, with a narrow dark eye stripe and a bright crimson rump. Its bill is blue-grey, despite the waxbill family’s association with red, wax-like bills.

avibase-F04B5608.name: Grey Wren
avibase-F04B5608.text: Grey covers the head, back and underparts. Dark bars across the tail add a little pattern.

avibase-50C8A5CF.name: Ground Parrot
avibase-50C8A5CF.text: It feeds on the ground among thick heathland and sedges. Green feathers marked with black and yellow help it disappear into the low vegetation.

avibase-BDA1AC35.name: Ground Tit
avibase-BDA1AC35.text: Once called a ground jay, this bird turned out to belong with the tits. Genetic studies helped reveal the relationship, despite its very different shape and life on the Tibetan Plateau.

sources.title: James et al. (2003): Pseudopodoces humilis is a tit, not a corvid
Gill et al., 2005: Phylogeny of Titmice

avibase-D1B9D410.name: Ground Woodpecker
avibase-D1B9D410.text: This woodpecker works the ground on rocky, open slopes. It digs into ant nests and probes them with a long, sticky tongue.

avibase-BF20B94D.name: Hill Pigeon
avibase-BF20B94D.text: At home on high rocky slopes, this pigeon breeds above 3,000 metres in the Himalayas. A broad white band crosses its dark tail.

sources.title: Zoological Survey of India: Fauna of Pin Valley National Park

avibase-8FCDB881.name: Hill Swallow
avibase-8FCDB881.text: A swallow of upland India and Sri Lanka, often seen over the hills. Its range includes India’s Western Ghats and Sri Lanka’s high country.

sources.title: Institute of Biology Sri Lanka: Phylogenetic affinities of Hill Swallow

avibase-FF41B79F.name: Lesser Cuckoo
avibase-FF41B79F.text: In Japan it is called hototogisu, a familiar bird in haiku. The poetry magazine Hototogisu, first published in 1897, takes its name from this cuckoo.

sources.title: National Diet Library, Japan Search: Lesser Cuckoo (Hototogisu)

avibase-60EA3FA9.name: Little Cormorant
avibase-60EA3FA9.text: About 51–56 cm long, this is a small cormorant with a short neck and a compact, hook-tipped bill. Breeding birds have fine pale streaks on the crown.

sources.title: Journal of Field Ornithology: Nest partitioning in a mixed-species waterbird colony
Iqbal et al. 2013: Little Cormorant breeding in Sumatra, Kukila 17

avibase-F2858F9F.name: Little Egret
avibase-F2858F9F.text: Small by egret standards, but still 55–65 cm long. It is a different species from the much larger Great Egret.

avibase-215FEA89.name: Little Grebe
avibase-215FEA89.text: This small grebe has a rounded, fluffy rear. In the breeding season its cheeks and throat turn chestnut, adding colour to its brown plumage.

avibase-F89FD6E3.name: Little Gull
avibase-F89FD6E3.text: The smallest gull in the world. An adult is about 28 cm long.

avibase-9A7B268C.name: Little Owl
avibase-9A7B268C.text: A full-grown Little Owl is only 21–23 cm long. “Little” describes the species, not a young owl.

avibase-4D28A0CD.name: Little Swift
avibase-4D28A0CD.text: This small swift has conspicuous white patches on the throat and rump. Those two pale marks stand out against its otherwise dark plumage.

avibase-17310BF0.name: Little Tern
avibase-17310BF0.text: The UK’s smallest tern has a yellow bill tipped with black. During courtship, the male carries a fish as the pair climbs and glides through the air.

avibase-7149F93D.name: Malachite Kingfisher
avibase-7149F93D.text: A pale blue crown barred with black sits above orange cheeks and rusty underparts. Adults have a red bill; young birds start with a dark one.

sources.title: Phil Hockey: Africa’s Kingfishers, University of Cape Town archive

avibase-26F27894.name: Malachite Sunbird
avibase-26F27894.text: The breeding male gleams metallic green and trails long central tail feathers. Females are olive-grey above and paler below, without his long tail.

sources.title: Biodiversity and Development Institute: Malachite Sunbird

avibase-84F096F7.name: Mangrove Cuckoo
avibase-84F096F7.text: Mangroves are a familiar home, though it also lives in other woods, even dry forest. A dark eye mask and warm buff belly help distinguish this long-tailed cuckoo.

avibase-837E6B04.name: Mangrove Hummingbird
avibase-837E6B04.text: This hummingbird lives only on Costa Rica’s Pacific coast. Its mangrove home is a narrow meeting place between coastal forest and the sea.

avibase-6C439FF4.name: Mangrove Warbler
avibase-6C439FF4.text: Mangroves are a good place to look for this yellow warbler. Some males have a chestnut cap, others a whole chestnut head; the migratory American Yellow Warbler is a separate species.

avibase-5BFEFD9A.name: Mountain Buzzard
avibase-5BFEFD9A.text: Mountain forests in East Africa are home to this buzzard. Its brown back and blotched pale underside suit the familiar buzzard pattern; the mountain part of its name is a useful habitat clue.

avibase-A61FDDF3.name: Mountain Kingfisher
avibase-A61FDDF3.text: Mountain Kingfishers live in New Guinea at higher elevations than their similar relative, the Yellow-billed Kingfisher. The mountain part of the name is a useful distinction between these two birds.

avibase-1FFFEF4E.name: Mountain Plover
avibase-1FFFEF4E.text: The name is misleading: this plover breeds on open, dry plains. Short grass and bare ground suit it better than mountain slopes or the wet shores associated with many other plovers.

avibase-C752BDF3.name: Mountain Robin
avibase-C752BDF3.text: This robin lives in New Guinea’s mountain forests. Researchers recorded it at about 3,000 metres on the Huon Peninsula, a fitting setting for a bird with mountain in its name.

sources.title: Freeman and colleagues, Bulletin of the British Ornithologists’ Club (2013)

avibase-8E286BF9.name: Mountain Thrush
avibase-8E286BF9.text: This brown thrush lives in mountain forests from Mexico to Panama. Older accounts called the same species Mountain Robin; the scientific name, Turdus plebejus, keeps the two English names connected.

sources.title: American Ornithological Society, Check-list species account

avibase-747B3A52.name: Mountain Wagtail
avibase-747B3A52.text: Rocky streams, including those in African mountains, suit this wagtail. A grey back and black-and-white wings frame an especially long tail, while a narrow dark band crosses the pale breast.

avibase-7DB7D6CE.name: Moustached Babbler
avibase-7DB7D6CE.text: The moustache is a fine grey stripe beside the bill. Brown feathers cover the back and wings, while the pale underside makes that small facial marking easier to pick out.

avibase-0A563359.name: Moustached Barbet
avibase-0A563359.text: Look for a narrow dark stripe beside the bill: that is the moustache. Green covers most of this barbet, with blue on the face adding another colour to inspect.

sources.title: Photograph by Francesco Veronesi from Italy

avibase-803B79B9.name: Moustached Kingfisher
avibase-803B79B9.text: A blue-purple stripe runs across the orange face like a moustache. Blue wings repeat that colour, while the large red bill adds another bright feature to the bird in the photograph.

avibase-5D5C6D51.name: Moustached Wren
avibase-5D5C6D51.text: White facial stripes give this wren a moustached look. A dark line borders the pale moustache below, while another pale stripe runs above the eye; the back is warm brown.

avibase-A091D50A.name: Northern Harrier
avibase-A091D50A.text: Its northern breeding range includes Alaska, Canada and the northern United States. Many travel south for winter, so “northern” does not mean they stay in the far north all year.

avibase-DF526047.name: Northern Wheatear
avibase-DF526047.text: “Wheatear” has nothing to do with wheat. It comes from an older name referring to the bird’s white rump, which flashes above a black-and-white tail when it flies.

avibase-02E004AD.name: Olive Woodpecker
avibase-02E004AD.text: Olive-green and bronze tones cover the back and folded wings. The grey head and bright red rump interrupt the green, so olive describes much of this woodpecker rather than every feather.

sources.title: Photograph by Nigel Voaden from UK

avibase-8897A0C5.name: Ornate Flycatcher
avibase-8897A0C5.text: White marks beside the bill and a bright yellow belly make this flycatcher look decorated. A partly hidden yellow crown patch adds another detail that may escape a quick glance.

sources.title: Peru Aves, Ornate Flycatcher field account

avibase-86D1B826.name: Ornate Pitta
avibase-86D1B826.text: A green back and blue wing patch contrast with a dark hood. Black and red on the belly add to this pitta’s ornate pattern.

sources.title: Yue et al. (2020): Species limits in the Elegant Pitta complex

avibase-8885A375.name: Ornate Sunbird
avibase-8885A375.text: The male combines a glossy blue throat with a yellow underside. Females lack that shiny throat. Older books may place this bird within the Olive-backed Sunbird, before that group was divided into several species.

avibase-1EA96AE1.name: Pied Harrier
avibase-1EA96AE1.text: “Pied” fits the adult male’s contrasting black and white plumage. Females are browner, so the bold pattern in the species name does not describe every individual equally well.

avibase-2D0ED462.name: Pied Heron
avibase-2D0ED462.text: A white neck and throat stand against a dark slate-coloured body and head. Young birds lack the dark cap and crest, so they can look surprisingly different from the pied adults.

avibase-1AE95762.name: Pied Monarch
avibase-1AE95762.text: The bird in the photograph wears a white collar between a black head and dark chest band. A white belly continues the pied pattern, with a blue ring around the eye.

avibase-FC943B05.name: Pied Plover
avibase-FC943B05.text: Black-and-white markings around the head and breast suit the word pied. Warm brown wings, red legs and a red ring around the eye make the rest of the bird less monochrome.

avibase-AC0C3921.name: Pied Thrush
avibase-AC0C3921.text: In this photograph, black and white patches cover the head, breast and wings, with dark spots scattered over the pale belly. The yellow bill is a bright exception to the pied pattern.

avibase-2FB34D83.name: Pied Wheatear
avibase-2FB34D83.text: A pale crown and belly contrast with the dark face and throat in this photograph. That bold arrangement of light and dark feathers makes the word pied easy to understand.

sources.title: Photograph by Ron Knight from Seaford, East Sussex, United Kingdom

avibase-7C3959D6.name: Plain Nightjar
avibase-7C3959D6.text: Plain at a glance, but finely patterned up close: grey and brown feathers carry dark mottling and narrow pale lines. There is more detail here than the name might suggest.

sources.title: Photograph by Jan Ebr & Ivana Ebrová

avibase-C4BD9E16.name: Plain Pigeon
avibase-C4BD9E16.text: Plain is relative: its head and breast carry a wine-red wash, with blue-grey on the rump and pale edges on the folded wings. The colours reward a closer look.

avibase-2FFB2DBC.name: Plain Sunbird
avibase-2FFB2DBC.text: Muted olive and grey tones make this sunbird plainer than many relatives. The male still has a small metallic blue-green band on the forehead, a detail easy to miss.

avibase-59A5A24E.name: Plain Swift
avibase-59A5A24E.text: Dark brown feathers make a nearly unbroken silhouette. The photograph shows long, pointed wings, with little bright colour or bold pattern to interrupt its plain appearance.

avibase-A874F334.name: River Tern
avibase-A874F334.text: Rivers are a good clue to this tern’s habits. It favours freshwater and often nests on sandy islands or riverbanks, though researchers have also recorded colonies in brackish lakes.

avibase-DF1E2A1D.name: Ruddy Duck
avibase-DF1E2A1D.text: The breeding male earns the reddish description with a chestnut body, set off by a bright blue bill. White cheeks and a dark cap complete the face in this photograph.

avibase-6647508A.name: Ruddy Kingfisher
avibase-6647508A.text: Rust-red feathers, a red bill and red legs make ruddy a useful description. On the back, the colour takes on a purple cast that contrasts with the warmer head and underside.

avibase-F4F72BD9.name: Ruddy Pigeon
avibase-F4F72BD9.text: Warm reddish-brown feathers cover the back and wings, with a wine-coloured wash over the breast. The understated pattern leaves those ruddy colours as the main feature to look for.

avibase-082099D1.name: Scarlet Robin
avibase-082099D1.text: The adult male wears a vivid scarlet breast beneath a black head. Females have a much softer reddish wash, so the colour in the name is strongest in the male.

avibase-42101632.name: Scarlet Tanager
avibase-42101632.text: Scarlet describes the breeding male: a red body with black wings and tail. Females are yellow-olive, and males become greener outside the breeding season while keeping their dark wings.

avibase-A28D8D38.name: Snowy Albatross
avibase-A28D8D38.text: Also known as the Wandering Albatross. Juveniles are mostly chocolate-brown, with white faces and underwings. They become whiter as they age.

sources.title: New Zealand Birds Online, Susan Waugh

avibase-AA7901D8.name: Snowy Egret
avibase-AA7901D8.text: White feathers give this small egret its snowy appearance. Its black bill and legs end in bright yellow feet, a useful detail when several white herons share the same wetland.

avibase-5B23B360.name: Snowy Owl
avibase-5B23B360.text: White plumage suits the Arctic setting, but many Snowy Owls have dark brown markings. Adult males tend to become whiter; females and young birds usually carry more pattern.

avibase-4976BF1D.name: Sooty Albatross
avibase-4976BF1D.text: Dark brown feathers give this albatross its sooty look. A narrow white crescent above and behind the eye and a yellow-orange line along the bill interrupt the dark colouring.

avibase-14D82446.name: Sooty Babbler
avibase-14D82446.text: Sooty-brown feathers have a subtle purple-bronze sheen, with a paler throat breaking up the darkness. Researchers rediscovered this limestone-forest bird in Vietnam in 1994 after decades without a recorded sighting.

sources.title: Bird Conservation International, Eames and colleagues (1995)

avibase-67D43542.name: Sooty Gull
avibase-67D43542.text: In breeding plumage, the dark brown head and grey-brown back suit the name “sooty”. A white half-collar breaks up the dark feathers.

avibase-C9B6F34C.name: Sooty Owl
avibase-C9B6F34C.text: Dark grey feathers give this owl a soot-dusted look. Fine white spots speckle the plumage.

avibase-9054A7CA.name: Sooty Swift
avibase-9054A7CA.text: Brown plumage gives this swift its sooty look. A paler forehead breaks up the darkness, without the frosted appearance of the similar Great Dusky Swift.

avibase-3E7F825D.name: Sooty Tern
avibase-3E7F825D.text: Sooty above, pale below: this ocean-going tern has dark upperparts but a white belly and forehead. Young birds are darker underneath, with white spots across the back.

avibase-C43110B3.name: Sooty Thrush
avibase-C43110B3.text: Dark brown feathers cover most of this thrush. The orange bill and legs stand out against the sooty body, and a pale eye adds a small, sharp point of contrast.

avibase-0A1A1F0F.name: Speckled Hummingbird
avibase-0A1A1F0F.text: Small dark specks cover the pale underside. A dark cheek patch and pale stripe above it add more pattern, while green and bronze tones appear on the back and wings.

avibase-A6EA9F02.name: Speckled Pigeon
avibase-A6EA9F02.text: White spots scatter across reddish-brown wings, making the speckled part of the name easy to see. A red patch around the eye supplies a much brighter block of colour.

sources.title: Photograph by peterichman from York, Yorkshire

avibase-A68B1787.name: Speckled Warbler
avibase-A68B1787.text: Buff streaks cross a dark crown, while the pale underside is heavily marked with black. Several kinds of fine pattern share the space suggested by the name speckled.

avibase-92F622EE.name: Vermilion Tanager
avibase-92F622EE.text: Vermilion is a vivid red, and this bird has plenty of it. A black throat and dark wings interrupt the bright red head and body shown in the photograph.

avibase-0ADA5F17.name: Western Tanager
avibase-0ADA5F17.text: Western fits its breeding range in western North America. A breeding male has a red face and yellow body, with black wings crossed by pale bars.

avibase-E35448DE.name: White Hawk
avibase-E35448DE.text: The white head and body are the first things to notice. Dark feathers remain on the wings, making the name a good first impression rather than a promise of an entirely white bird.

avibase-400E032C.name: White Wagtail
avibase-400E032C.text: White is only part of the pattern. In this photograph, pale cheeks and belly sit beside a black throat, a grey back and black-and-white wings.

sources.title: Photograph by Jac. Janssen from BAARLO LB, NL

avibase-5CA0BA87.name: White Woodpecker
avibase-5CA0BA87.text: A white face and underside contrast with black wings. Look around the eye for a yellow ring, a small splash of colour on an otherwise mostly black-and-white woodpecker.

avibase-5BC4E0EF.name: Willow Flycatcher
avibase-5BC4E0EF.text: Willows and other waterside shrubs are typical breeding habitat for this small flycatcher. It catches insects in the air or picks them from leaves, so both halves of the name offer useful clues.

avibase-F963401E.name: Willow Tit
avibase-F963401E.text: Damp, young woodland suits this tit in Britain, including places with willows. It digs its own nest hole in soft, decaying wood, so the trees provide more than a perch.

avibase-27B2749A.name: Wood Duck
avibase-27B2749A.text: Woodland ponds and swamps suit this duck, which usually nests in a tree cavity. The young leave the elevated nest by jumping down, often the morning after they hatch.

avibase-C21A0347.name: Wood Pipit
avibase-C21A0347.text: Miombo woodland and other grassy woodland suit this African pipit. It searches the undergrowth for insects and other small invertebrates, giving the wood in its name a useful habitat connection.

sources.title: Biodiversity Explorer, Roberts Birds of Southern Africa account

avibase-F600592A.name: Yellow Grosbeak
avibase-F600592A.text: A yellow head and body contrast with black-and-white wings in this photograph. The large, deep bill is just as striking as the yellow plumage when you look at the bird’s face.
